title: “Therefore, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline. Monks,…
content: “Therefore, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline. Monks, just as near a village or small town there is a large sala-tree forest overgrown with trumpet-flower creepers. Then a man comes who desires the welfare of that forest, its benefit, its security from bondage. He cuts down the crooked, weak branches, throws them out, and cleans the forest inside. He properly cares for the straight, well-grown sala saplings. Monks, after some time, that forest becomes grown, prosperous, and increased. So too, monks, abandon the unwholesome and strive for the wholesome states. Thus you will achieve growth, prosperity, and increase in this Dhamma and Discipline.”

title: “Monk, ‘ant-hill’ is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent,…
content: “Monk, ‘ant-hill’ is a synonym for this body composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished with rice and porridge, impermanent, subject to rubbing, pressing, breaking, disintegration, dissolution. ‘Smoking by day and blazing by night’—what belongs to daytime work, reflected upon at night—that is ‘smoking by night.’ What, after reflecting at night, is practiced during the day by body, speech, and mind—that is ‘blazing by day.’ ‘Brahmin’ is a synonym for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘Wise man’ is a synonym for a monk in higher training. ‘Sword’ is a synonym for noble wisdom. ‘Digging up’ is a synonym for arousing effort, striving. ‘Door-bolt’ is a synonym for ignorance; ‘lifting the door-bolt’ means abandoning that ignorance. ‘The wise man, taking the sword, dug up’ is the meaning.”

title: “Monks, there are these four ignoble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging seeks what is subject to aging; being…
content: “Monks, there are these four ignoble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging seeks what is subject to aging; being himself subject to sickness seeks what is subject to sickness; being himself subject to death seeks what is subject to death; being himself subject to defilement seeks what is subject to defilement. These, monks, are the four ignoble searches.”

title: “Monks, I will teach you about things that are bound and about binding. Listen. And what, monks, are the things that are bound? What is…
content: “Monks, I will teach you about things that are bound and about binding. Listen. And what, monks, are the things that are bound? What is binding? Form, monks, is a thing that is bound. Desire and lust for form is the binding of form. Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness, monks, is a thing that is bound. Desire and lust for consciousness is the binding of consciousness. These, monks, are called the things that are bound. This is the binding.”

title: “Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. A first point cannot be discerned of beings wandering and roaming on, shrouded by ignorance and bound by…
content: “Monks, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. A first point cannot be discerned of beings wandering and roaming on, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving. It is possible, monks, that the great ocean might dry up, be exhausted, and cease to exist. But I say that beings shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, wandering and roaming on, will not have made an end of suffering. It is possible, monks, that Sineru, the king of mountains, might be destroyed and cease to exist. But I say that beings shrouded by ignorance … will not have made an end of suffering. It is possible, monks, that the great earth might be destroyed and cease to exist. But I say that beings shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, wandering and roaming on, will not have made an end of suffering!”

title: Venerable Udaya: “I have come with a question — To the meditator, sitting dustless, Duty done, without defilements, Who has reached the far shore —…
content:
Venerable Udaya:
“I have come with a question —
To the meditator, sitting dustless,
Duty done, without defilements,
Who has reached the far shore —
Speak the knowledge of liberation,
The breaking of ignorance.”

The Blessed One replied to Udaya:
“Abandon desire for sensual pleasures,
Both sorrow and grief;
Abandon sloth and torpor,
And prevent remorse.

Knowledge of liberation, I say,
Is the breaking of ignorance —
Purified by equanimity and mindfulness,
With reflection leading the way.”

Venerable Udaya:
“What binds the world?
What is its range?
By abandoning what is Nibbāna called?”

The Blessed One:
“The world is bound by delight;
Directed thought is its range.
By abandoning craving,
Nibbāna is called.”

title: “Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A…
content: “Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A boil, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Clinging, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A bog, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. And why, monks, is fear a synonym for sensual pleasures? Monks, infatuated by sensual desire, bound by sensual desire, one is not free from fear in this very life, nor free from fear in the future. Therefore, fear is a synonym for sensual pleasures.”

title: “Monks, while Prince Vipassī was going to the pleasure garden, he saw a sick person, suffering, gravely ill, wallowing in his own urine and feces,…
content: “Monks, while Prince Vipassī was going to the pleasure garden, he saw a sick person, suffering, gravely ill, wallowing in his own urine and feces, needing others to lift him, needing others to support him. Seeing this, the prince asked the charioteer: ‘Good man, what has this person done that his eyes are not like those of others, his voice not like others?’ ‘Your Highness, that is called a sick person.’ ‘Good man, why is he called a sick person?’ ‘Your Highness, he is called a sick person because he has not recovered from his illness.’ ‘Good man, then am I subject to sickness, not having fallen sick yet?’ ‘Your Highness, you and I as well — all of us are subject to sickness, even though we have not fallen sick yet.’ ‘Good man, then this visit to the pleasure garden is enough. Drive back to the palace.’ ‘Yes, Your Highness.’ Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove back to the palace. Monks, Prince Vipassī returned to the palace, suffering, grieving, and thought: ‘Shameful indeed is this birth! And anyone who is born must also age, must also be sick!’”

title: Elder Nun Sumedhā: Even if there were seventeen treasures, Filling the ten directions completely, Sensual desires are never satisfied — One dies, still unsatisfied. Sensual…
content:
Elder Nun Sumedhā:

Even if there were seventeen treasures,
Filling the ten directions completely,
Sensual desires are never satisfied —
One dies, still unsatisfied.

Sensual desires are like swords and spears,
Sensual desires are like a snake’s head,
Like a blazing torch,
Like a smooth-gnawed bone.

Sensual desires are not permanent,
Nor are they everlasting —
Much suffering, a great poison,
Like a red-hot iron ball —
The source of misfortune,
Resulting in suffering.

Sensual desires are like a fruit tree,
Like a piece of meat — trouble,
Like a dream, like a illusion —
Sensual desires are like borrowed goods.

Sensual desires are like swords, like stakes,
Disease and boils,
Misfortune and agitation —
Like a pit of glowing embers —
The source of misfortune,
Fear and destruction.

Fools, for a long time,
Weep in this wandering continuation.
From beginningless time until now,
They weep at being subject to death,
Weep for slain brothers,
Weep for being slain themselves.

Remember from beginningless time —
Tears, milk, and blood
Flow in saṃsāra,
Without ever stopping.
Remember the accumulation of bones
Of beings wandering on.

Remember the four oceans
Filled with tears, milk, and blood —
Remember the bones of one lifetime,
As high as Vepulla.

Remember from beginningless time —
Not enough to make
The whole Jambudīpa
As a heap of mustard seeds
Of mothers and fathers in saṃsāra.

Remember from beginningless time —
Grasses, trees, branches, leaves —
Not enough to contain
A four-fingered pot
For the fathers in saṃsāra.

Remember the image
Of the blind turtle in the eastern sea,
Poking its head into
The hole of a floating yoke —
To illustrate
How hard it is to be human.

title: “Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for…
content: “Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for the tongue … for the body … for the mind is a defilement of the mind. When a monk has abandoned these defilements in regard to these six sense bases, his mind inclines to renunciation. Having been fully saturated with renunciation, his mind becomes wieldy and he directly knows the things to be fully known.”
